item.description: Comparing 112 primary care clinicians given Nuance's DAX Copilot ambient documentation with 103 similar clinicians without it over 180 days, Atrium Health found no significant difference in electronic health record time or financial measures, with small reductions in documentation time only in exploratory subgroups of heavy users, low-volume clinicians and family medicine. Atrium Health was the first health system to use DAX Copilot. Clinicians using it were recruited between June and August 2023 and compared with clinicians from similar practices who did not, and electronic health record use and financial outcomes were modelled with linear mixed models over 180 days, controlling for length of use, age, gender, provider type, years in practice and baseline. The primary analyses were not significant. Exploratory analyses found small decreases in documentation hours for high users, who transferred at least 60% of DAX notes (means ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.88-0.98), for low-volume clinicians (0.91, 0.83-0.99) and for family medicine (0.91, 0.85-0.98). The study was funded by Wake Forest University Health Sciences and registered as NCT06329427. Lab: Atrium Health. Model: DAX Copilot (Nuance, Microsoft), since renamed Dragon Copilot. Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Lean proofs of security properties for the compiled machine code of libsignal
item.description: Google DeepMind's AlphaProof Code, a framework in which humans vet Lean specifications and Gemini-powered agents write the proofs, produced about 6.5 million lines of Lean establishing forward secrecy, authentication, post-compromise security and handshake secrecy for Signal's PQXDH handshake and Triple Ratchet as compiled to AArch64 machine code from unmodified libsignal, along with machine-checked disproofs for two previously fixed bugs reintroduced into the code. The verified program is libsignal-cli, a small harness around the unmodified libsignal v0.105.4 and SPQR crates built by stock rustc, and the theorems are stated over whole runs of its AArch64 executable, so neither the Rust source nor the compiler is trusted. Humans and models wrote the specifications together, with a human reviewing each one; prover agents then wrote proofs that a gatekeeper accepted only when Lean's kernel checked them against the approved statement using standard axioms, with sorry and native_decide rejected. Reviewer agents flagged about one percent of the proof code for human review, and the work took four weeks. The two reintroduced bugs, a small-subgroup key encoding and a weak-state splicing attack, were found earlier by Cheval, Jacomme and Richards; for each the system proved the buggy binary insecure. The Lean development is public. Lab: Google DeepMind. Model: AlphaProof Code agents powered by Gemini Carbon. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: AI-led.

item.title: Three prototype electronic devices designed by Claude Fable 5.2 and built by Diode Computers
item.description: From short prompts, Claude Fable 5.2 wrote the specifications, schematics, four-layer circuit board layouts, enclosures, firmware and parts lists for a USB speakerphone, a voice-assistant hub and a handheld virtual pet; Diode Computers, which has a disclosed commercial relationship with Anthropic, built all three from Claude's design files without changes to the circuitry, and all three still worked after weeks of use. Each device began from a one-sentence prompt naming the device and its main hardware requirements. Claude placed components, routed copper with high-speed and noise-sensitive connections first, revised layouts on its own when routing stalled, and for the hub wrote its own grid-search router when KiCad's one-track-at-a-time router proved too slow. It ran design-for-manufacturing and parts-availability checks itself, modelled the enclosures in CAD, checked board-to-enclosure fit in code (finding that the speakerphone board must be tilted about 25 degrees to install), and shortened the hub's microphone ports to move their resonance out of the voice band. Diode reports that it manufactured the boards with no rounds of manufacturing changes. The post also reports internal benchmark gains over earlier Claude models, which are not the result recorded here. Lab: Anthropic / Diode Computers. Model: Claude Fable 5.2. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: AI-led.

item.title: Gait embeddings from a single depth camera predict health phenotypes across 18 body systems
item.description: A gait foundation model that turns three-dimensional skeletal motion, recorded by a single depth camera during five motor tasks, into learned embeddings predicted age (r = 0.69), body mass index (r = 0.91) and visceral fat area (r = 0.83) better than engineered gait features in 3,328 deeply phenotyped adults, significantly predicted 1,887 of 3,210 tested phenotypes, and improved on a baseline of age, body mass index, visceral fat and height in all 18 body systems in men and 17 of 18 in women, including clinical diagnoses and medication use. Gait is usually summarised by engineered measurements such as cadence and stride length and read as a sign of particular diseases. Here the model encodes how all body joints move together over time, and those embeddings were tested against thousands of phenotypes measured in the Human Phenotype Project cohort, from grip strength to sleep quality. Ablations that removed body regions found leg dynamics carried most of the metabolic and frailty signal and torso dynamics most of the sleep and lifestyle signal. The authors argue for gait as a passive, multisystem vital sign in routine clinical assessment. Lab: Weizmann Institute of Science. Model: Gait foundation model producing learned embeddings of 3D skeletal motion; architecture not named in the abstract. Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Explainable machine-learning decision support for diabetic foot ulcers, externally validated and tested in a randomised comparison
item.description: An ensemble of gradient-boosted trees and neural networks trained on records of 763 diabetic foot ulcer patients at two Chinese hospitals predicted cure, recurrence, amputation and death at a third hospital with a macro-averaged AUC of 0.901; in a 202-patient randomised comparison of AI-assisted against usual care, the AI-assisted arm had better short-term follow-up engagement and glucose-management adherence, and blinded experts scored AI-assisted versions of usual-care recommendations higher than the clinicians' originals (7.77 against 6.47 out of 9). Development used electronic records and follow-up from 2018 to 2025 at two hospitals in Jiangsu and Anhui, with a locked model then tested on 100 patients from a hospital in Shandong; discrimination was highest for amputation (AUC 0.953) and death (0.951) and lowest for recurrence (0.820). From January to March 2026, 202 patients were randomised 1:1. In the AI-assisted arm physicians drafted a plan without the tool, then reviewed the four predicted risks, SHAP explanations and AI-generated recommendations through a web platform before revising, and kept final authority; the tool added about four minutes of data entry and two minutes of review per encounter. In the usual-care arm physicians worked without it. Lab: Affiliated Hospital of Xuzhou Medical University / Westlake University. Model: Ensemble of single-task XGBoost and multilayer perceptron models with SHAP explanations. Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: A machine-learning microexon splicing code links rare variants to autism in 7,391 families
item.description: A gradient-boosted classifier trained to recognise neuronally spliced microexons from their surrounding sequence was used to score variants in whole genomes from three autism cohorts, prioritising 72 variants associated with autism within families that occur in 2.5% of autistic individuals and in none of their unaffected siblings; minigene assays in human induced neurons confirmed that representative variants alter microexon splicing. Microexons are 3 to 27 nucleotide exons, mostly in neuronal genes, whose splicing is often disrupted in autistic brains. The study first profiled bulk and single-cell RNA-sequencing data to find 1,514 previously unknown human microexons and 1,115 mouse ones, then trained the classifier to separate sequences around true neural microexons from microexon-like background, so that a variant's effect on splicing can be scored as a change in the model's output. Applied to the SSC, SPARK and MSSNG cohorts (25,132 individuals in 7,391 families), rare and ultrarare variants had the largest predicted impact, the most affected microexons recurred across all three cohorts, and the 72-variant set comprises 28 ultrarare variants prioritised by this model and 44 also prioritised by DeltaSplice, an independent splicing predictor. About 82% of carriers had no previously detected candidate variant, and the variants concentrate in synaptic genes. Lab: University of Toronto. Model: Gradient-boosted decision trees (XGBoost) microexon code-model. Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Computer-assisted proof of a uniform spectral gap for the spin-1 Heisenberg chain on even periodic rings
item.description: A manuscript in OpenAI's October 2026 mathematics release proves that the spin-1 antiferromagnetic Heisenberg chain on even periodic rings has a unique ground state and a spectral gap above (log 20)/784 ≈ 0.0038 for every even length L ≥ 2304, the periodic formulation of Haldane's 1983 conjecture, by combining an analytic thermal-purity argument with certified finite computations. Haldane predicted in 1983 that integer-spin antiferromagnetic chains have a gap above the ground state while half-integer chains do not; numerics put the spin-1 gap near 0.41, but no proof existed for the Heisenberg chain itself, which is not frustration free, so the finite-size criteria used for models such as AKLT do not apply. The manuscript, dated 24 September 2026 and published on 6 October 2026 as result 268 of the openai/math release that this registry records at 2026-10-06-openai-math-collection, bounds the gap through the purity of the Gibbs state, propagating finite-ring partition-function bounds to all longer even rings; it also gives Δ_L≳4.79 × 10⁻⁴ for L ≥ 60. A companion manuscript treats open chains with boundary fields. The release ships a Python finite verifier for the numerical inputs and no Lean formalization of this result. Three outside papers have since built on the proof: Sirui Lu's tensor-network reformulation sharpens the bound to Δ_L > 0.0729 for every even L ≥ 36 from the same inputs and certifies gaps for seven further chains and ladders, Hal Tasaki uses its machinery to prove uniqueness of the translation-invariant ground state of the infinite chain, and Tarun Grover extends the purity bootstrap to higher dimensions and fermions. Lab: OpenAI. Model: Unreleased internal OpenAI model, not named in the release. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: AI-led.

item.title: Metasurface colour router inverse-designed with a neural-network-accelerated genetic algorithm, fabricated and measured
item.description: A U-Net trained on 140,000 finite-difference time-domain simulations stood in for the solver inside a genetic algorithm, which evaluated 4 × 10⁷ candidate layouts for a single-layer silicon nitride colour router over a 2 µm Bayer cell; the fabricated device measured 88.8% total transmission against 95.4% predicted, though with per-colour routing efficiencies and crosstalk worse than simulated. Camera sensors filter colour by absorption, discarding most incoming light; a colour router instead steers red, green and blue light onto their sub-pixels. The design here is a 16 by 16 grid of 600 nm silicon nitride pillars at 125 nm pitch. The surrogate predicts full transmitted field maps about 2.3 × 10⁵ times faster than the solver, which let the search run 4,000 generations against the roughly ten thousand structures a solver-driven genetic algorithm can afford. Because it predicts fields rather than a single score, the same trained network can be reused for other photodiode aperture layouts without new training data. In a colour-chart reconstruction using the measured spectra, the router gave brighter images than a literature colour-filter-array response at some cost in spatial resolution. Lab: Chungnam National University. Model: U-Net surrogate (about 4.9 million parameters) inside a genetic algorithm. Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: Search scaffold.

item.title: Randomised trial of AI-ECG guided monitoring for undetected atrial fibrillation
item.description: In a single-centre trial in Taiwan, 14,665 adults without known atrial fibrillation were randomised to have their past year of sinus-rhythm ECGs analysed by an AI model, with the 1.1% it called high risk offered up to seven days of Holter monitoring, and the composite of newly detected atrial fibrillation, flutter or pre-atrial-fibrillation findings at 90 days was 0.74% against 0.48%, a result the authors describe as statistically fragile. Atrial fibrillation often goes undetected until a stroke, and the attraction of an AI-ECG model is that it claims to see a signature of atrial vulnerability on an ordinary ECG recorded in sinus rhythm, when nothing is visible to a reader. Adults aged 40 to 85 with no previous atrial fibrillation or flutter were randomised to an AI-ECG-guided strategy or usual care, 7,337 against 7,328. Within the intervention arm, participants whose ECGs from the preceding year were scored high risk were offered Holter monitoring; 84 participants (1.1%) were flagged and 48 of them (57.1%) were monitored. The design deals with the obvious bias that monitoring finds what monitoring looks for: each monitored participant was paired with an age- and sex-matched control chosen before the control arm's ECGs were analysed, and those controls received identical monitoring, with reporting cardiologists blinded to the AI results and to allocation. The primary composite occurred in 54 intervention participants against 35 controls, an odds ratio of 1.54 (95% CI 1.01 to 2.37, P = 0.046), and the effect was concentrated as designed, at 32.1% against 2.6% among high-risk participants and 0.4% against 0.5% among the rest. Lab: National Defense Medical Center, Taiwan. Model: An institutional AI-ECG model scoring atrial electrical vulnerability from sinus-rhythm ECGs. Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Randomised trial of a risk model triaging patients with a positive antinuclear antibody test
item.description: At one US academic health system, 2,385 people with a new positive antinuclear antibody test were randomised to a pathway in which an electronic health record risk model invited those it scored high risk to expedited rheumatology evaluation, and those in the intervention arm reached an autoimmune disease diagnosis faster, with a median of 43 days against 138. A positive antinuclear antibody test is common and mostly uninformative, and no evidence-based rule existed for deciding which of these patients should see a rheumatologist. The model was built in 2024 from a chart review of 2,000 positive-antinuclear-antibody patients using demographics, billing codes for autoimmune symptoms and laboratory values, reaching an area under the curve of 0.83 in training and 0.75 in validation, and was then embedded in the health record. In this two-year pragmatic study every patient with an incident positive test was randomised 1:1 independently of their risk score; in the intervention arm high scores triggered an invitation to expedited rheumatology evaluation, while in the control arm scores were computed and not acted on. Both arms received standard care and could be referred as usual, and chart review every six months recorded evaluations and diagnoses. Of 2,385 randomised, 954 intervention and 1,006 control patients were analysed after postrandomisation exclusions, and time from positive test to diagnosis favoured the intervention arm with a hazard ratio of 1.9 (95% CI 1.3 to 2.7, P < 0.001). Lab: Vanderbilt University Medical Center. Model: An interpretable electronic health record risk model for systemic autoimmune disease, developed by the same group in 2024. Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Randomised trial of AI feedback on clinicians reading fetal Doppler ultrasound images
item.description: 96 clinicians at five Danish hospitals were randomised to receive AI feedback or none while judging 40 standardised umbilical and middle cerebral artery Doppler vignettes each, and those given feedback were accurate on 75.0% of vignettes against 62.3% without it, a difference of 12.7 percentage points measured against expert consensus rather than patient outcomes. Umbilical and middle cerebral artery Doppler measurements guide management of fetal growth restriction, and their reliability depends heavily on who is holding the probe. Residents, gynaecologists and obstetricians were randomised 1:1 and matched into 48 pairs by obstetric ultrasound experience, each evaluating 40 vignettes built from pre-existing static Doppler images, 1,920 unique vignettes in all. For colour Doppler images clinicians indicated where they would place the measurement gate, and for spectral images they judged whether the waveform was technically adequate, both components of a valid measurement. Intervention clinicians saw the unannotated image alongside the AI's feedback, then entered their own answer on the unannotated image. Accuracy was scored against consensus between two fetal medicine sonographers with more than ten years of experience, with a consultant resolving disagreements, using criteria based on International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology guidance. The authors report that clinical experience still mattered when the AI feedback was itself wrong, and frame the result as support for studying human and AI collaboration during real-time acquisition. Lab: University of Copenhagen, Technical University of Denmark and Copenhagen Academy for Medical Education and Simulation. Model: An explainable AI system giving visual and textual feedback on Doppler gate placement, anatomical suitability, insonation angle and waveform quality (not named). Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Refutation of the k-Clique hypothesis, independent of the matrix multiplication exponent
item.description: Two complexity theorists working back and forth with ChatGPT-6 published an algorithm that counts weighted k-cliques faster than the long-conjectured barrier for every large enough k, and faster even if matrix multiplication were optimal, with the paper crediting the decisive algebraic decomposition almost purely to the model. The k-Clique hypothesis holds that the 1985 Nesetril-Poljak reduction is optimal, so that finding a k-clique needs about n^(ωk/3) time, where ω is the matrix multiplication exponent. It is load-bearing in fine-grained complexity: hardness results for parsing, compressed-data problems and many other tasks are proved by reduction from it. The paper gives an algorithm running in n^((ω/3 − c)k) time for a constant c > 0 that does not depend on ω or k, so the refutation survives even in the ω = 2 limit, and it counts weighted k-cliques rather than only detecting one. The engine is a rank-or-swap decomposition that the authors then rewrote in purely combinatorial form, used as a black box inside a human-built algorithmic framework that only needs square matrix multiplication. Lab: Independent (MIT and Tel Aviv University). Model: ChatGPT-6 (OpenAI), public web interface, no harness. Verification: Author verified. Autonomy: Collaborative.

item.title: LLM agents write quantum programs checked against Lean specifications
item.description: Google DeepMind and Google Quantum AI report that teams of language model agents, searching against frozen Lean specifications that an external verifier re-checks, found quantum programs that cut published resource costs by up to 290 times for fixed-point arcsine and by factors of 11, 8 and 2.5 on simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug metabolism. Quantum algorithms cannot be tested empirically at the scales that matter, because a classical computer can only simulate small instances, so the paper replaces testing with proof. Researchers write a problem as a Lean file stating the target correctness and cost theorems with the program, its cost bound and their proofs left as sorry placeholders, then launch independent agent teams with generic optimization prompts rather than problem-specific ideas. Teams share a wiki of best verified solutions and reusable lemmas and meet in scheduled forum conferences where unverified conjectures count for nothing. Because an agent can edit files in its own workspace, every submission is replayed in a clean sandbox by an external verifier using the Lean Comparator, which confirms that the theorem statements and every definition they depend on are unchanged and that the proof terms use only propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice with no sorry and no added axiom. Reported reductions are 1.41 times for expected oracle rounds in parallel Grover search, more than 290 times in spacetime cost for fixed-point arcsine, and 10.9, 8.08 and 2.49 times on the three scientific simulations. Lab: Google DeepMind / Google Quantum AI. Model: Not named: the paper says only that large language model agents synthesize the programs. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: Search scaffold.

item.title: Hypertension detected from consumer smartwatch sensors without a cuff
item.description: A Google model reading photoplethysmography and accelerometer signals from a consumer smartwatch, with no cuff calibration, flagged hypertension in 196 prospectively enrolled participants with 65.8% sensitivity and 90.0% specificity against 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring, slightly ahead of initial office blood pressure screening at the same specificity. More than half of adults with hypertension do not know they have it, and the condition produces no symptoms to prompt a measurement. The model takes the optical pulse and motion waveforms a smartwatch already records during ordinary wear, with no blood pressure cuff used to calibrate it to the individual, and was evaluated in a prospective multicentre study of 196 participants free of known cardiovascular disease and not taking antihypertensive medication, against 24-hour ambulatory monitoring as the reference standard, over seven days of real-world wear. It reached sensitivity 65.8% (95% CI 54.0 to 76.3), specificity 90.0% (95% CI 83.2 to 94.7) and positive predictive value 80.6% (95% CI 68.6 to 89.6), where initial office blood pressure screening in the same study reached sensitivity 55.3% at the same specificity. The authors frame the use as opportunistic screening that prompts people toward a clinical assessment and cuff-based confirmation, not as a measurement of blood pressure. Lab: Google Research. Model: AI-PPG-ACC-HTN. Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Gradient-boosted early warning score tested for clinical net benefit across 2.08 million Danish hospital encounters
item.description: Across 2,080,765 encounters at 15 Danish hospitals, a gradient-boosted model using vital signs, laboratory values and text embeddings of medical history beat the National Early Warning Score for predicting death within 24 hours by 1.9 additional correct identifications per 10,000 patients overall, a gain that rose to 78.1 per 10,000 among patients the existing score already called high risk and fell to 0.9 per 10,000 among those it called low risk. Early warning scores are recalculated at the bedside across most hospital systems, so the question of whether a machine learning model is worth substituting is a practical one, and the paper's contribution is to ask it in terms of clinical net benefit rather than discrimination alone. The cohort covers every adult encounter with at least one score recorded at 15 hospitals in ten networks between 2018-10-16 and 2023-10-16, 825,200 unique patients in all, followed until death or 24 hours after the first score. The comparison runs in both directions, against a simplified score dropping blood pressure and temperature and a demographic variant as well as against the full machine learning model, with propensity score weighting used to blunt the bias introduced when staff intervene on a high score and prevent the death the score predicted. The headline finding is that model complexity bought very little on average and that the average hides the useful result: among patients whose first score was 7 or above the model added 78.1 correct identifications per 10,000, while the simplified score lost 60.2, and among those scoring 0 to 4 all three approaches were within one per 10,000 of each other. The authors read this as an argument for risk-stratified monitoring rather than for replacing the score outright. Lab: University of Copenhagen and Capital and Zealand region hospitals. Model: XGB-EWS, an XGBoost model over vital signs, demographics, laboratory markers and sentence-transformer embeddings of medical history. Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: AI agent search raises 1,873 entries of the Grassl qubit code tables
item.description: A search written and run by AI agents under one physicist's direction produced 192 explicit quantum stabilizer codes whose minimum distance beats the best bound previously recorded for their parameters, raising 1,873 entries of the standard reference table, with every distance certified exactly and a checker published alongside. Grassl's tables at codetables.de record, for every length up to 256 and every dimension, the best known bounds on the minimum distance of a qubit stabilizer code, and more than half the entries above length 100 give a lower bound with no explicit code behind it. The construction here takes a random Clifford encoder and expurgates it: every logical operator of weight below the target distance is enumerated, and a few are promoted to stabilizers so each low-weight one anticommutes with at least one promoted operator. That yields 192 codes between lengths 53 and 254 at distances 5 to 13, 161 beating the listed lower bound by one and 31 by two, which propagate to 1,873 raised table entries. A first-moment count explains why it works, since expurgated random codes carry about eight more logical qubits than a typical random code of the same length and distance, and predicts gains at 619 further parameter pairs. The work was done during a three-day hackathon at Argonne National Laboratory, with the heavy computation on the Aurora supercomputer. Lab: Virginia Tech. Model: Not named: the paper and repository say only that AI agents wrote and ran the search. Verification: Author verified. Autonomy: Collaborative.

item.title: Claimed Diophantine definition of ℤ in ℚ
item.description: Elliot Glazer, working with four frontier models, published an explicit integer-coefficient polynomial whose rational zeros project exactly onto the integers, which if correct would refute Mazur's conjecture on the topology of rational points and give a second route to the undecidability of Hilbert's tenth problem over the rationals. A set is Diophantine in ℚ when membership can be written as the existence of rational witnesses satisfying a polynomial equation. Julia Robinson defined ℤ in ℚ in 1949 using both quantifiers, and Koenigsmann later gave a universal definition, but a purely existential one stayed open and Mazur's conjecture on the real closure of rational points would have ruled it out. The repository gives a construction in 292,890,231,905 variables and two smaller quartics, one in 411 variables with every coefficient written out in decimal and one in 394 variables written against the fixed integer C = 3^2²⁵, and argues that degree four is the minimum possible. The work builds on OpenAI's October 6 preprint, which claims the undecidability of Hilbert's tenth problem over ℚ by a different route that does not produce a Diophantine definition of the integers, and credits a rank-one elliptic curve strategy going back to Thanases Pheidas and a prime-pattern strategy to Zhi-Wei Sun. Lab: Independent. Model: Astra 6, Sol 6.1 and Opus 5.5, with auditing from Fable 5.1. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: Collaborative.

item.title: The Stacks Project formalized in Lean by directed AI agents
item.description: Axiom Math released a Lean formalization of the whole Stacks Project, the roughly 7,500-page reference work on algebraic geometry, at about 16 million lines with no sorry, and says its agents found dozens of statements in the original text needing repair, including a lemma on algebraization of coherent formal modules that the library marks as false as published. The Stacks Project, started by Johan de Jong in 2005, is an open-source reference whose every item carries a permanent four-character tag. The release formalizes every tag with formalizable content on top of Mathlib, preserving the tag structure so each Lean declaration links back to the canonical text, and tagging declarations with the EGA and SGA items they prove. The library is split into two tiers: StacksCore, which a person has checked against the source and brought to Mathlib standards, and StacksFrontier, written by AI agents and not yet reviewed, with Lean's kernel checking every proof in both and only the three standard axioms permitted. Axiom says agents diagnosed the obstructions behind failed proof attempts and built explicit counterexamples, and the repository carries them as named files: StacksFrontier records that tag 0EJA is false as published because its proof identifies a dimension function with the dimension of a closure using a result that needs A/I catenary, and gives a pinched Noetherian local domain as a counterexample, alongside principal-ideal and two-generator counterexamples to a canonical map on sections away from a closed subset. Lab: Axiom Math. Model: AxiomProver agent swarms using an unnamed mix of models. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: Collaborative.

item.title: Randomised trial of a maternal health chatbot finds no improvement in anxiety or depression at 12 months
item.description: 400 pregnant and postpartum people from racially and ethnically minoritised groups across 49 US states were randomised to Rosie, a generative AI maternal health chatbot, or to monthly children's books, and after 12 months the chatbot arm showed no improvement in anxiety or depression scores, nor in emergency department visits, postpartum care, contraception use or sleep. Chatbots are widely proposed to fill the gap in support after delivery, when contact with the health system drops away while medical and psychological needs continue, and this trial is one of the few to measure whether one changes anything a year out. Participants were recruited online, enrolled between October 2023 and December 2024 with follow-up completed in December 2025, and randomised 1:1 against an active control receiving monthly children's books. The chatbot was built with community-engaged methods and answered questions from a shared knowledge base rather than tailoring responses by race or ethnicity, and it carried an automated safety alert for messages suggesting distress or urgent symptoms, reviewed by a clinical social worker who contacted the participant. Primary outcomes were the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 and Patient Health Questionnaire-9 at 12 months, and both were null: an adjusted mean difference of 0.10 (95% CI -0.77 to 0.96) for anxiety and -0.23 (95% CI -1.05 to 0.59) for depression. The authors conclude that such chatbots may be better positioned as adjunctive tools than as stand-alone interventions. Lab: University of Maryland. Model: Rosie, a generative AI maternal health chatbot answering from an evidence-based knowledge base (underlying model not named). Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-led.

item.title: First text read in the Herculaneum scroll PHerc. 306B
item.description: Two Vesuvius Challenge contestants combined a public ink-detection model with one they fine-tuned themselves to recover readable Greek from PHerc. 306B, a carbonised Herculaneum scroll nobody had read, where the papyrology team agreed on the phrase "that which is in itself desirable". PHerc. 306 was buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79, excavated in the 1750s and micro-CT scanned in 2025, and is broken into two parts. Identifying ink in the larger part, PHerc. 306B, also settled which part is which: the script orientation shows 306B is the upper section of the original roll. A surface inside the scan was grown with VC3D's GrowPatch tool from a seed on a line found by screening windings, then ink was called only where two models agreed, by multiplying the output of the public TRACE v3B model with a model the pair fine-tuned from Youssef Nader's v8-in, trained half on labels from a different scroll and half on machine labels averaged from four public models, with an added penalty for marking blank papyrus as ink. The sequence τoδιαυτo had been visible in several submissions for about a month, but the following letters were read as either mu, nu or alpha-iota until this image made a diagonal middle stroke visible and the papyrology team agreed on alpha-iota, giving a reading with parallels in Aristotle, Sextus Empiricus and Philodemus' On Anger. Twenty-five submissions were reviewed on this scroll and several others reached 7 to 9 characters against a 10-character target. Lab: Vesuvius Challenge. Model: TRACE v3B with a fine-tuned derivative of the v8-in ink model, plus VC3D GrowPatch segmentation. Verification: Author verified. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Designed transcriptional activation domains, over 90 percent functional in yeast
item.description: A Berkeley-led team generated 500,000 candidate activation domains, scored them with existing machine learning models including three neural networks, and synthesized 18,750 of the top ones, of which more than 90 percent worked as activation domains in yeast, with some retaining function in fungi, plants and human cells. Protein design has worked best on structured proteins, where a fold constrains the sequence. Activation domains are the opposite case: they are intrinsically disordered regions of transcription factors that recruit coactivators, with weak structural constraints and poorly defined sequence-to-function rules, which makes them a test of whether a prediction-and-screen loop can design disordered sequence at all. Candidates resembling known activation domains were generated computationally, scored by several extant predictors, and 18,750 high scorers were measured in yeast, of which 16,770 gave clean measurements and over 90 percent functioned. Sequences that several models agreed on were stronger, which is what motivated MADRIGAL, the fast consensus predictor the paper then builds. Designed domains that keep working across fungi, plants and human cells matter for synthetic biology, agriculture and biotechnology, where an activation domain is a reusable part. Lab: University of California, Berkeley. Model: Existing activation-domain function predictors including three neural networks, plus MADRIGAL, a consensus predictor built from the results. Verification: Author verified. Autonomy: Search scaffold.

item.title: A self-improving agent selected antibiotic candidates at nearly twice a prior expert workflow's hit rate
item.description: MoLRSI, an agent that rewrites its own molecular-discovery workflows using memory of earlier tasks, built a screening workflow whose 107 selected compounds hit at 15.9% against Staphylococcus aureus, against 8.7% for the same group's earlier expert-designed workflow on the same training data and the same 12-million-compound library, and separately produced eight experimentally validated peptide-MHC binders. The paper's own framing is an agent architecture that optimizes workflows and model architectures and carries memory across tasks, which on its own would be out of scope here; what brings it in is the wet-lab validation. For antibiotics the agent assembled its own activity and cytotoxicity predictors, screened a library of 12,076,365 compounds drawn from the Mcule purchasable database and the Broad Institute collection, and selected 107 compounds for testing, two of which, C3 from ChemBridge and C32 from Vitas-M, were characterized for minimum inhibitory concentration against methicillin-sensitive and methicillin-resistant S. aureus and for cytotoxicity against HepG2, HSkMC and IMR-90 cells. The comparator is the same laboratory's earlier expert-led workflow, which tested 241 compounds from the same library using the same training data. In the second setting the agent designed de novo binders to HLA-A*02:01 presenting the MART-1 and SARS-CoV-1 peptides, with designs synthesized and displayed on phage, yielding eight hits that preferred their intended target over the off-targets tested, while a comparator protocol run with Claude Science yielded none. Lab: Northeastern University / Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard. Model: Claude Sonnet 5 as the MoLRSI backbone; Claude Opus 5 for the Claude Science comparator. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: Search scaffold.

item.title: Designed full-length IgG antibodies against 22 targets, including GPCR agonists
item.description: Pythia Labs reports that its all-atom generative model designed full-length human IgG antibodies for 22 therapeutic targets, and that screening at most 48 candidates per target after a single design round found single-digit nanomolar binders, including both agonists and antagonists of G protein-coupled receptors. Therapeutic antibody discovery is slow, gives little control over how an antibody engages its target, and has struggled with whole target classes, G protein-coupled receptors above all, where the binding site is in the membrane and the conformational state matters. The pipeline generates candidates directly in full-length human IgG format rather than as fragments, conditioning on human germline frameworks and applying sequence constraints meant to avoid known developability liabilities, and reasons over sequence and atomic structure together under explicit design constraints, which is what the paper credits for being able to aim at a specified epitope and conformational state. Reported results are single-digit nanomolar affinities for soluble proteins and single-digit nanomolar cell-binding EC50 values for GPCRs, with single-digit nanomolar inhibitory potency in functional assays for several targets, and biophysical profiles the paper calls comparable to or better than clinical-stage controls. The lead sequences are published so others can test them. Lab: Pythia Labs. Model: Pythia-1, an all-atom generative model over sequence and structure jointly. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: Search scaffold.

item.title: Randomised trial of an AI management platform for breast cancer patients on home CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy
item.description: In a three-arm randomised trial across hospitals in Tianjin, 189 breast cancer patients taking CDK4/6 inhibitors at home were assigned to an AI management platform, a tailored active follow-up service by phone and text, or standard care; a preprint reports that both active arms kept anxiety and depression scores better than standard care, without reporting a comparison between the AI and the human follow-up. The registration describes the platform as a 24-hour service added to routine follow-up, offering emotional companionship, medication reminders and adverse-reaction assessment against CTCAE standards. The second arm received personalised phone calls and text messages from a follow-up centre, and the third routine advice and education. Primary outcomes were the Self-Rating Anxiety and Depression Scales at 24 weeks, with EORTC QLQ-C30 quality of life and patient-reported adverse events (PRO-CTCAE) secondary. Of 189 randomised, 161 were analysed (53 AI, 54 follow-up, 54 standard care). Both intervention arms did better than standard care on anxiety and depression (both P ≤ 0.001) and on cognitive, emotional and social functioning and global health, while scores in the standard-care arm worsened, with depression peaking at week 16. The authors also report that the AI arm captured more patient-reported adverse events. Lab: Tianjin Medical University Cancer Institute and Hospital. Model: Zhiliao Doctor AI management platform. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Deep learning marker of mortality risk from retinal photographs, validated in three external cohorts (RetiME)
item.description: A deep learning marker that maps a retinal photograph directly to an individual's mortality risk, trained on a European cohort, was associated with all-cause and cause-specific mortality and with the later onset of a wide range of systemic and eye diseases in three external cohorts in Southeast Asia, Eurasia and North America, and was used to reconstruct personalised lifespan trajectories. Retinal Mortality Equivalent (RetiME) was built on large foundation models and trained to read individual mortality risk from low-cost, non-invasive retinal photographs. Beyond a static risk estimate, the authors use it to reconstruct a personalised lifespan trajectory for each person, and report that these trajectories were associated with observed outcomes such as age at death. Clustering the trajectories separated cancer-predominant, cardiometabolic and neurodegenerative patterns. Interpretability analyses and a genome-wide analysis, which identified loci associated with RetiME, are offered as evidence that it captures biology rather than image artefacts. Lab: National University of Singapore and Singapore Eye Research Institute. Model: RetiME, a deep learning marker built on large foundation models (not named in the abstract). Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Pediatric posterior fossa tumour classifier from T2 MRI with abstention, evaluated at an outside site (PedDx)
item.description: A preprint reports a classifier for five pediatric posterior fossa tumour types from a single T2-weighted MRI, which abstains when unsure, reaching 81.4% accuracy on 129 external cases (88.7% when it did not abstain) and 92.5% on 40 cases run through the full workflow by a team at another institution, while degrading on out-of-distribution scans, sometimes confidently. The classifier separates medulloblastoma, ependymoma, atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumour, low-grade glioma and diffuse midline glioma without needing a tumour segmentation. It was trained on 492 treatment-naive scans from the Children's Brain Tumor Network and CHOP and tested on 114 held-out replication cases (79.8%, or 90.5% among cases where it did not abstain), and on 129 cases from Children's Healthcare of Atlanta. A team at Macquarie University ran the deployed workflow, which produces a prediction and a structured quality-control report, on 40 cases from the Women's and Children's Hospital in Adelaide. The authors also tested 236 out-of-distribution cases, including post-treatment scans, artefacts and tumour types never seen in training, and found degraded performance with confidently wrong predictions, plus sensitivity to acquisition and alignment perturbations. Lab: Children's Hospital of Philadelphia. Model: PedDx, a frozen 3DINO vision transformer with a classification head, calibrated, with confidence-based abstention. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Smartphone profile photograph screening for skeletal malocclusion, externally validated in Turkey and Belgium
item.description: A preprint reports that a classifier using 100 geometric features from a single side-profile smartphone photograph, with no radiograph, kept its sensitivity for skeletal Class III malocclusion across two external cohorts but lost specificity in a non-European cohort from a Belgian clinic, where its AUC fell from 0.902 to 0.835, and fell further in a second task separating Class I from Class II (0.875 to 0.723). Two binary tasks were evaluated, Class III against the rest and Class I against Class II, each with its own development set and model, applied unchanged at the default threshold. The reference standard was the ANB angle on pre-treatment lateral cephalograms traced by orthodontists, never shown to the model. One external cohort came from a Turkish university orthodontic department outside the development set (256 patients in the Class III task) and the other from a private orthodontic clinic in Brussels described as non-European (282 patients). For Class III, sensitivity was similar across the evaluation sets (0.801, 0.836 and 0.848), while specificity fell from 0.766 to 0.697. Sensitivity was lower in children than in adults in both cohorts (0.71 to 0.80 against 0.89 to 0.90). Lab: Bezmialem Vakif University, Muğla Sıtkı Koçman University and Kedi Mobil Uygulama. Model: Geometric machine learning classifiers on 100 engineered facial-profile features. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Lean-checked construction of four-dimensional quantum Yang-Mills theory by OpenAI, without uniqueness or a mass gap
item.description: OpenAI's language model produced a Lean proof, since released and rebuilt by an independent committee of physicists and mathematicians, that a relativistic quantum field theory satisfying the Wightman axioms arises as a scaling limit of four-dimensional Wilson lattice gauge theory for every simple compact gauge group; the committee judges this an existence proof for pure Yang-Mills theory, while uniqueness of the infinite-volume limit and the mass gap remain unproved. OpenAI asked David Gross on 16 October 2026 to take custody of the proof, and Gross formed a shepherding committee with Michael R. Douglas, Arthur Jaffe, Igor R. Klebanov and Nikita Nekrasov, whose two-page statement hosted by the Kavli Institute described a 1147-page argument building on Wilson's 1974 lattice regularization and Balaban's rigorous renormalization group. The committee published the Lean sources of OpenAI's 28 October submission on 5 November and, on 10 November, a 35-page initial assessment with its own checks in yang-mills-group/YM. On its reading the proof builds continuum correlation functions of gauge-invariant polynomials in the curvature as scaling limits of Wilson lattice correlations at fixed physical volume, extracts an infinite-volume limit along a subsequence by compactness, splits the limit into pure phases that each satisfy the Osterwalder-Schrader axioms, and reconstructs a Wightman theory, with a conserved stress tensor obeying its Ward identity, a nonzero trace with the expected leading short-distance law, an operator product expansion with error bounds and a proof that the theory is not free. The committee rebuilt the 9,470 project modules cleanly under Lean 4.32.0, found no project axioms, no use of sorryAx and no unsafe declarations among 250,319 imported declarations, and replayed the 100,168 declarations behind the 17 principal results in a fresh kernel using only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. Comparator passed against OpenAI's public theorem on 30 October, against the committee's own stronger combined target on 3 November and against a separate operator-product statement on 5 November, and further Lean adapters show that the construction satisfies Osterwalder-Schrader axioms formulated before the committee knew of it (xiyin137/OSreconstruction) and that its finite Wilson measure equals the one in an independent lattice gauge theory formalization (mrdouglasny/lgt). Lab: OpenAI. Model: OpenAI language model, not named in the committee's statement. Verification: Formally verified. Autonomy: AI-led.

item.title: Non-uniqueness of unforced two-dimensional Euler flows with unbounded integrable vorticity
item.description: A two-part manuscript by Matei P. Coiculescu, whose detailed proofs, code and text were largely produced with Claude Opus 5.5 under his direction, claims that the incompressible Euler equations in the plane, with no external force, admit two distinct renormalized weak solutions from the same radial initial vorticity, which lies in L¹ ∩ L^q for every q < ∞ but is unbounded; Part I is on arXiv and the whole proof is formalized in Lean. One solution is the stationary radial vorticity itself. The other is 3-fold rotationally symmetric, equimeasurable with the datum at every time, and leaves it in finite time; the two differ in Lₜ^(∞)(L¹ ∩ L^q)ₓ for every q ∈ (4/3, ∞) and every large enough time horizon. Part I proves two ingredients: a compactness criterion, under which radial data approximated by 3-fold symmetric solutions whose non-radial moment stays bounded below yield a second solution, and a linear analysis showing an unstable eigenvalue for the linearization around the basic building block plus a small point vortex. Part II, the nonlinear construction, is in the repository but not on arXiv. The repository's Lean 4 development, about 1,280 files and 170,000 lines, proves that a three-part Hypothesis (N) implies the main theorem, proves (N3) directly, and proves sound a checker for the computer-assisted parts (N1) and (N2). Those were certified twice: by a Python program in rigorous ball arithmetic (FLINT/Arb), and by a compiled run of the Lean checker on 2026-10-22 that took 8.75 hours and printed true on all 261 cells. Lab: Independent. Model: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic). Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Lean formalization of interior gradient Hölder estimates for infinity-harmonic functions
item.description: Juan J. Manfredi machine-checked in Lean one of the result families in OpenAI's October 2026 mathematics release, a uniform interior estimate giving every bounded viscosity solution of the infinity-Laplace equation on the unit ball of ℝᵈ, d ≥ 3, a gradient that is Hölder continuous on the half ball, and with it the corollary that every infinity-harmonic function on a connected open set in those dimensions is C¹; the Lean proofs and the blueprint were written by Claude under an AI-assisted formalization pipeline. The infinity-Laplace equation Δ_(∞)u = ∑uᵢuⱼuᵢⱼ = 0 arises as the limit of the p-Laplace equation and governs absolutely minimizing Lipschitz extensions. How smooth its solutions are has been open away from the plane: Savin proved planar solutions are C¹ in 2005, and Evans and Smart proved in 2011 that solutions are differentiable everywhere in every dimension, but neither a uniform gradient bound nor C¹ regularity was known for d ≥ 3. The OpenAI manuscript of 4 October 2026 claims both: for every d ≥ 3 there are α ∈ (0, 1/3] and a finite C with sup|∇u| + [∇u]_(C^(0, α)) ≤ C osc u on the half ball for every bounded viscosity solution on the unit ball, and as a consequence that every infinity-harmonic function on a connected open subset of ℝᵈ is C¹. The formalization carries all three of the manuscript's results, the estimate, the corollary and the Liouville theorem for the degenerate limiting equation on space-time that the proof rests on, as InfHarmonic.main_estimate, InfHarmonic.interior_C1 and InfHarmonic.liouville, proved from Mathlib and including the Crandall-Ishii-Lions theorem of sums and Alexandrov's theorem used along the way. It is pinned to Lean v4.35.0-rc2 and the matching Mathlib release, and the README reports no sorry outside the statement file and no axioms beyond the three standard ones. Lab: Independent. Model: Claude, under the Trellis AI-assisted formalization pipeline; the underlying manuscript came from an unreleased internal OpenAI model. Verification: Formally verified. Autonomy: AI-led.

item.title: Erdős Problem 654 answered negatively by Google DeepMind's Aletheia agent
item.description: An agent built on Gemini Deep Think produced an elementary counterexample showing that n points in the plane with no four on a circle need not contain any point having (1 − o(1))n distinct distances to the others, a negative answer to Erdős Problem 654 as the problem database formulates it; that construction has since been proved in Lean, and so has the negative answer by a second, different construction. Write f(n) for the largest number such that every set of n points in ℝ² with no four on a circle contains a point at f(n) or more distinct distances from the rest. Erdős asked in his 1997 problem collection whether f(n) > (1 − o(1))n, the trivial bound being f(n) ≥ (n − 1)/3. Aletheia answered no: its counterexample places 2m points on each coordinate axis, at powers of 2 and 3, giving 4m points in which every point sees at most roughly 3n/4 distinct distances. The paper reports 13 problems marked open in the database addressed by the agent, some by novel solutions and some by locating solutions already in the literature, and its Table 1 classifies this one as a Partial AI Solution, meaning the problem carried several questions and the agent solved the first of them. An independent Lean 4 development by Daniel Veljjanoski, registered at Palomar on 2026-11-02, proves both the negative answer and the quantitative form, using a different set on the same two axes, the points (±2i, 0) and (0, ±(2j − 1)) for 1 ≤ i, j ≤ m, and finishing the no-four-concyclic condition by parity rather than by unique factorization. A second development by the GitHub user ukniusanqian-alt, registered at Palomar on 2026-11-03, proves the same two statements with Aletheia's own set, the points (0, ±3^(k + 1)) and (±2^(j + 1), 0) for 0 ≤ j, k < m, which are the paper's points with the exponents re-indexed from {10, …, m + 9}, and closes the no-four-concyclic step as the paper does, through the power of the origin, ending by comparing an odd product with an even one. Lab: Google DeepMind. Model: Aletheia, a mathematics research agent built on Gemini Deep Think. Verification: Formally verified. Autonomy: AI-led.

item.title: Sixty-three previously unrecognised Oracle Bone duplicates found with an image-matching system
item.description: OBD-Finder, an image-matching system from Henan University that ranks candidate duplicates among published copies of Shang dynasty Oracle Bone inscriptions, led its developers' Oracle Bone specialists to 63 pairs of records that show the same bone but had not been recognised as duplicates, released with catalogue numbers and plates in January and February 2025 and reported in a refereed EMNLP 2026 demonstration paper. Oracle Bone fragments were dispersed among collections and published repeatedly over a century, so the same bone often appears in several catalogues under different numbers, and recognising those duplicates (校重) is basic curation: it fixes counts, traces provenance and exposes forgeries. OBD-Finder compares hand copies by low-level keypoint matching, then by character-level similarity, and ranks candidates for a specialist to inspect. Run over Huang Tianshu's Oracle Bone Inscription Copy Series of about 60,000 copies, it found 101 duplicate groups, of which the team announced 45 as new on 2025-01-11, by what it called an incomplete tally, and 18 more on 2025-02-23, each listed by catalogue number with plates. The arXiv preprint followed in May 2025, and the EMNLP 2026 System Demonstrations paper entered the ACL Anthology on 2026-10-24. The work has since continued at larger scale: in July 2026 a revised OBD-Finder 2.0 compared the Heji Bubian supplement with the Heji corpus, Zhang confirmed 881 duplicate groups by hand, and after subtracting the duplicates already catalogued by Cai Zhemao, Men Yi and Ding Junwei, 115 were reported as new. Lab: Henan University / LMU Munich. Model: OBD-Finder: keypoint matching with EAST character detection and a Siamese network. Verification: Author verified. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Randomised trial of voice-guided AI navigation for biliopancreatic endoscopic ultrasound
item.description: In a single-centre randomised trial of 266 patients in China, a real-time AI system that recognises scanning stations and prompts the endoscopist by voice raised the completeness of guideline-recommended biliopancreatic endoscopic ultrasound stations from a median of 0.81 to 1.00, while lengthening procedures by about two minutes. EUS-GUIDEQ was developed from 27,072 annotated images from 189 patients, with station classification accuracy of 94.2% on 1,500 internal images and 78.8% on 2,062 multicentre external images. Between December 2023 and May 2025 patients were randomised 1:1 to AI-assisted or standard examination, with 132 and 134 analysed. The primary endpoint, completeness of standardised scanning stations adjudicated by blinded experts from recorded video, was a median of 1.00 (interquartile range 0.94 to 1.00) against 0.81 (0.75 to 0.88), P < 0.001, with benefit across participating endoscopists. Procedure time was 12.70 against 10.55 minutes, and no serious procedure-related adverse events occurred. Lab: Central South University (Third Xiangya Hospital). Model: EUS-GUIDEQ. Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Weak normalization implies strong normalization in pure type systems with βη-conversion, proved in Lean
item.description: A Lean proof, written by Claude Opus 5.5 under four authors' direction by adapting OpenAI's proof of the β case, that in every pure type system with βη-conversion, if every legal term is weakly normalizing then every legal term is strongly normalizing, the βη form of a conjecture Geuvers stated in 1993. The Barendregt-Geuvers-Klop conjecture asks whether weak normalization implies strong normalization in every pure type system; Geuvers states it for all of them in his 1993 thesis as Conjecture 8.1.2. OpenAI's release of 6 October 2026 included a preprint and Lean proof of the case where the conversion rule uses β-conversion only, family 245 of the collection recorded at 2026-10-06-openai-math-collection. This development proves the βη case for every specification, with no functionality, finiteness or decidability assumed: weak βη-normalization of every legal term implies strong βη-normalization, and so does weak β-normalization. Because an η-step can delete a λ-annotation, the proof works from the weaker property that every legal term has a β-reduct with no β-redex outside its λ-domains, handles conversion through domain erasure, indexes candidates by βη-normal forms of erased types and makes observation values η-canonical. OpenAI's 33 Lean files for the β case are copied in and ported to Lean v4.35.0. Lab: Independent. Model: Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, adapting an OpenAI Lean proof of the β case. Verification: Formally verified. Autonomy: Collaborative.

item.title: Measurably isomorphic Bernoulli shifts with different base entropies, proved in Lean
item.description: A Lean proof, registered on Palomar, that some countable group has measurably isomorphic Bernoulli shifts over alphabets of different sizes, so that base entropy is not an isomorphism invariant for that group; the group comes from OpenAI's claimed counterexample to Kaplansky's direct-finiteness conjecture, and the dynamical construction was written with GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6 Sol under Peter Burton's direction. For a countable group G and a finite alphabet A, the Bernoulli shift is G acting by translation on A^G with the uniform product measure. Ornstein showed in 1970 that base entropy is a complete invariant of these shifts over the integers, and Bowen showed in 2010 that it is an isomorphism invariant over every sofic group, so shifts with different base entropies can be isomorphic only over a group outside that class. The registered theorem gives a countable group G and a nontrivial finite alphabet A for which the shifts on A and on A × A are equivariantly isomorphic on invariant conull sets, with a measurable inverse. The group and the algebraic input come from OpenAI's manuscript A Counterexample to Kaplansky's Direct-Finiteness Conjecture in Characteristic Two, whose abstract says the group is non-sofic; its Lean development is imported at a pinned commit, and this project builds the dynamical conjugacy on top of it. Lab: Independent. Model: GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6 Sol via Codex, building on an OpenAI construction. Verification: Formally verified. Autonomy: Collaborative.

item.title: System-wide AI scribe deployment and clinician documentation time at a 14-hospital health system
item.description: Across 1,637,227 outpatient encounters at a 14-hospital Boston health system, enrolment in the Heidi ambient AI scribe was associated with 1.21 fewer minutes of active note time per encounter, more among heavy users, and longer notes, with no change in same-day or after-hours note closure or in work relative value units. After system-wide availability from January 2025, 902 outpatient clinicians enrolled, of whom 605 used the tool and 297 did not. The study used an interrupted time series indexed on each clinician's enrolment month and adjusted for patient demographics and visit complexity, over notes from 1 July 2024 to 31 January 2026, with a secondary comparison of non-users, low users and high users. Note-active time fell by 1.21 minutes (95% CI 0.68 to 1.74) on enrolment and by 2.50 minutes among high users, and high users' notes grew by about 171 characters relative to non-users. Lab: Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center / Beth Israel Lahey Health. Model: Heidi (Heidi Health). Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Classification of Finite Simple Groups formalized in Lean by directed AI agents
item.description: Axiom Math released a sorry-free Lean proof of the Classification of Finite Simple Groups that follows the first-generation proof, about 43.1 million lines written over 24 days by swarms of AI agents directed by its mathematicians and engineers, whose agents also found counterexamples to a step in one published route to the Unbalanced Group Theorem. The classification states that every finite simple group is cyclic of prime order, alternating, of Lie type, or one of 26 sporadic groups. Its first-generation proof is spread over hundreds of papers and books, and the second-generation revision is incomplete, so the project formalized the first-generation proof. The README states the theorem through the classification statement of the TauCeti project, written outside Axiom, and says the proof builds on Mathlib and TauCeti with only Lean's three standard axioms and no native_decide. The announcement says about 1.2 million lines come from the Qiuzhen-CFSG project and that the work was split into 108 milestones and about 380 tasks, with lead agents decomposing arguments and reviewing the statements being formalized while other agents searched for existing results or wrote proofs. Formalizing Walter's argument, the agents found explicit counterexamples to a closure assertion it uses, and a companion paper by Colin Defant and Ken Ono gives an alternative argument for the simple-group case of the Unbalanced Group Theorem built on Solomon's 1976 theory of maximal 2-components, whose key step the announcement credits to AxiomProver. Lab: Axiom Math. Model: AxiomProver agent system using an unnamed, changing mix of models. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: Collaborative.

item.title: Sogge's local smoothing conjecture claimed in every dimension, with Bochner–Riesz and Kakeya as consequences
item.description: An OpenAI manuscript released with a Lean formalization claims Sogge's local smoothing conjecture for the wave equation in every spatial dimension, and from it the Bochner–Riesz conjecture, the Kakeya and Nikodym maximal conjectures, full Hausdorff dimension for every Euclidean Kakeya set, and Fourier restriction for the sphere, paraboloid and cone throughout the interior of the conjectured range. Local smoothing asks how much regularity solutions of the wave equation gain on average in time beyond what fixed-time estimates allow. Sogge conjectured the sharp form in 1991, and it was known to imply the Bochner–Riesz and Kakeya conjectures; Guth, Wang and Zhang proved it in two spatial dimensions in 2020. Family 079 of openai/math, added on 26 October 2026, pairs a manuscript dated 25 October with an earlier one claiming the critical L³ estimate in three dimensions. OpenAI's scope page says the Lean formalization bounds, for every n ≥ 2 and 2 ≤ p < ∞, the Lᵖ(ℝⁿ × [1, 2]) norm of the half-wave by the W^(s, p) norm of Schwartz initial data with s = max(0, (n − 1)/2 − n/p) + ε, and also gives uniform Bochner–Riesz bounds, spherical extension estimates and Stein square-function bounds in their strict ranges, the Kakeya maximal bound with δ^(−ε) loss, and full dimension for every set containing a unit segment in each direction. The release note says the model output is published directly, as in the release of 6 October. Lab: OpenAI. Model: Unreleased internal OpenAI model, not named in the release. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: AI-led.

item.title: Deep learning detection and staging of femoral head osteonecrosis on hip x-rays across six Chinese hospitals
item.description: OsteoAID, a YOLOv8-based model trained on 20,722 hip x-rays from 16,399 patients at six Chinese hospitals, staged osteonecrosis of the femoral head with 96.6% accuracy on an external test set, against 75.0% for radiologists. Expert orthopaedists annotated each image to separate osteonecrosis from radiographically similar conditions and graded confirmed lesions on the Ficat and Arlet scale, using images from 2015 to 2023. On the internal test set the model raised staging accuracy from 87.4% for the unmodified YOLOv8 network to 96.4%, with a detection mean average precision of 93.0% at an intersection-over-union threshold of 50%. It was compared with radiologists and orthopaedists on two external test sets, and with MRI-based staging, the reference standard, on a third. The authors propose it as a decision-support tool for triage. Lab: Sun Yat-sen University (with the Chinese Artificial Intelligence Project Group for Hip Joint Diseases). Model: OsteoAID (YOLOv8-based). Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Multiagent language-model and CNN system scores BT-RADS on glioma follow-up MRI
item.description: A system pairing a locally run 20-billion-parameter gpt-oss model, which extracts clinical variables from notes, with a scoring agent applying BT-RADS logic to tumour volumetrics classified 492 post-treatment glioma MRI examinations with 76.0% accuracy against an expert reference, against 57.5% for the initial clinical assessments. BT-RADS standardises response assessment after glioma treatment but requires combining imaging trends with medication effects and radiation timing. 509 consecutive examinations from 2017 to 2021 at one centre were evaluated retrospectively, 492 of them evaluable. Agreement with the reference had a Cohen kappa of 0.71. Sensitivity was high in categories that depend on clinical context (100% for BT-1b, 92.7% for BT-1a, 87.5% for BT-3a) and moderate in those that depend on thresholds (57.1% to 74.8%), and positive predictive value for BT-4 was 92.9%. Lab: Duke University Medical Center. Model: gpt-oss 20B (OpenAI, open weights) extractor agent with a convolutional neural network scorer. Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-led.

item.title: Chest radiograph model for prescreening reduced ejection fraction, tested in three Korean cohorts
item.description: DLLV, a deep learning model that flags a left ventricular ejection fraction of 40% or less on chest radiographs, reached AUCs of 0.86 in a tertiary-centre cohort and 0.92 to 0.97 in two health-checkup cohorts, and as a prescreen was estimated to cut echocardiography volume by up to 85% without missing any of the 19 affected people in those cohorts. The model was developed on 24,674 patients with 32,135 same-day radiograph and echocardiogram pairs from 2016 to 2021, using counterfactual learning to improve performance and the localisation of its heatmaps. External testing covered a tertiary referral cohort of 5,440 patients and two health-checkup cohorts of 28,034 and 6,085. In the checkup cohorts the area under the precision-recall curve was 0.04, which still corresponds to 87-fold and 37-fold enrichment over the low baseline prevalence. Lab: Seoul National University Bundang Hospital. Model: DLLV. Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: ECG deep learning ensemble separates Takotsubo syndrome from anterior STEMI and improves reader accuracy
item.description: A preprint reports an ensemble of three deep learning models that distinguished Takotsubo syndrome from acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction on 12-lead ECG images with 91.4% accuracy in a 95-person external cohort, and raised 70 healthcare providers' estimated probability of a correct diagnosis from 0.632 unaided to 0.864 with AI assistance. The models were pretrained self-supervised and fine-tuned on ECG images from two hospitals recorded within 14 days of symptom onset, with 832 participants for development and 95 for external validation, healthy controls included. External AUROC was 0.970. A four-phase reader study compared unaided reading, a reference sheet and AI assistance, then randomised readers on a new ECG set to the reference sheet alone, AI predictions, or AI predictions with Grad-CAM heatmaps, which gave a further gain. In exploratory analyses less experienced readers gained most, and cardiologists' unaided advantage reversed under AI assistance, which the authors frame as a utilisation bias hypothesis. Lab: North Medical Center Hiroshima City Asa Citizens Hospital. Model: Ensemble of three deep learning models with self-supervised pretraining. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Épi agent reports 120 record bounds and constructions, with released certificates
item.description: Bake AI's Épi agent, running GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra against fixed verifiers, reports 20 improved numerical bounds and 100 record constructions, including certificates that the Cohn–Elkies sphere-packing bound cannot be sharp in dimensions 10 and 11, an upper bound of 4.29569 on Klarner's polyomino growth constant against 4.5238, and a computer-assisted extension of Tuza's conjecture for a class of split graphs. Épi keeps a persistent research history across model sessions, branches and reviews its own work, and has each output scored by a fixed verifier, accepting an improvement only when it is feasible and clears a set margin over the literature value. The results repository lists 12 families of numerical bounds and 8 of constructions. The headline mathematics: dual certificates giving lower bounds on the Cohn–Elkies linear programme of about 0.0564 and 0.0577 in dimensions 10 and 11, above the known upper bounds on sphere-packing density there, so the method cannot be sharp in either; the bound λ ≤ 4.29569 for Klarner's constant, whose previous record was 4.5238 and whose empirical value is about 4.06; an interval for the n-queens constant about 84 times narrower than before; and a proof that τ_(△)(G) ≤ 2ν_(△)(G) for split graphs with an eight-vertex clique part and at most three active neighbourhood types, up from two. The construction records are mostly circle and ball packings, 46 of them circles in a quarter disk. Lab: Bake AI. Model: GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra in the Épi agent. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: Search scaffold.

item.title: AI-enhanced auscultation for left ventricular dysfunction, validated in prospective Japanese cohorts
item.description: An AI model reading digital heart sounds from four chest sites with a single-lead ECG detected an ejection fraction of 40% or less with an AUROC of 0.904 in an external prospective cohort of 964 patients, and was more accurate than a consensus of seven cardiologists in a 100-patient reader substudy (82.0% against 62.0%). Adults referred for clinically indicated echocardiography at multiple Japanese centres underwent digital auscultation with a simultaneous single-lead ECG, with same-visit echocardiography as the reference. The ensemble was trained on 2,359 patients, 8.9% with reduced ejection fraction, and validated on 964 from a separate multicentre registry, 7.6% with it. External sensitivity, specificity and accuracy were 86.3%, 74.2% and 75.1%. The model outperformed ECG-only models and clinical regression models including B-type natriuretic peptide, and a simplified two-site version kept an AUROC of 0.903. Lab: Juntendo University (with AMI Inc.). Model: Transformer and one-dimensional CNN ensemble over four-site digital auscultation and single-lead ECG. Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: RFdiffusion3 designs active phosphotriesterases and transthyretin-specific zinc proteases zero-shot
item.description: RFdiffusion3, a generative model that diffuses free atoms to satisfy atomic constraints, produced de novo phosphotriesterases with a two-metal active site and zinc proteases specific for transthyretin, obtaining active catalysts of both kinds from zero-shot design campaigns of 96 constructs. The method places individual atoms rather than residues, aiming to meet sets of atomic constraints such as an enzyme active site more quickly and accurately than earlier methods, across tasks from enzyme design to RNA structure design. The experimental demonstrations are two enzyme classes: phosphotriesterases whose active site includes a carbamylated lysine coordinating two metal ions, and zinc proteases that cut transthyretin, the protein involved in transthyretin amyloid disease. In both, a campaign of 96 constructs tested without iterative optimisation yielded active catalysts. Lab: Institute for Protein Design, University of Washington. Model: RFdiffusion3. Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: Search scaffold.

item.title: Randomised trial of AI-generated lay summaries before neurosurgical consultations
item.description: In a single-centre randomised trial of 300 outpatients in Dresden, giving patients a quality-checked AI-generated lay summary of their medical findings before consultation improved patient-rated quality of the physician-patient interaction (4.42 against 4.25 on the FAPI scale) and shortened median consultations from 33 to 25 minutes. Adults attending an outpatient neurosurgical clinic were randomised 1:1 to standard care with or without a layperson summary of their findings, produced by the Simply Onno tool and quality-checked before use. The primary endpoint, patient-reported interaction quality, improved by 0.17 (95% CI 0.05 to 0.29), driven by shared decision-making, with no difference in perceived empathy. Patients rated autonomy support higher while physicians rated their own slightly lower, and the ratio of geometric mean consultation times was 0.79 (0.70 to 0.88). Evidence for an increase in encounter difficulty was weak, and secondary intervals were not adjusted for multiplicity. Lab: TU Dresden (University Hospital Carl Gustav Carus). Model: Simply Onno (underlying model not named in the abstract). Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Integer multiplication below n log n, against the Schönhage–Strassen optimality conjecture
item.description: An OpenAI manuscript gives a deterministic algorithm that multiplies two n-bit integers in time O(n(log n)^(1 − κ)) with κ = 2⁻¹⁸² on a multitape Turing machine, which would beat the O(n log n) algorithm of Harvey and van der Hoeven and disprove Schönhage and Strassen's 1971 conjecture that n log n is optimal; David Harvey calls the claim plausible but says he has not checked it. Schönhage and Strassen conjectured in 1971 that multiplying n-bit integers needs on the order of n log n bit operations, and Harvey and van der Hoeven reached that bound in 2021. Family 109 of OpenAI's release claims an algorithm running in O(n(log n)^(1 − κ)) with κ = 2⁻¹⁸², exact at every input length on one fixed finite-alphabet Turing machine with finitely many one-dimensional tapes. The manuscript is dated 23 September 2026 and was published with the release of 6 October. Harvey's note of 20 October describes three closely related manuscripts, says the work builds directly on the 2021 algorithm, and reports that others had already lowered the exponent of log n to about 0.9983. He argues that the size of κ is beside the point, since saving a power of log n is exponentially larger than any earlier improvement in this line. Lab: OpenAI. Model: Unreleased internal OpenAI model, not named in the release. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: AI-led.

item.title: Locked AI model for p16/Ki-67 dual-stain triage validated on 9,006 cervical screening cases
item.description: Cytoreader-Fusion, an AI system that classifies p16/Ki-67 dual-stain cytology slides to triage HPV-positive screening results, was locked before validation and then detected biopsy-confirmed CIN 3+ with 88.3% sensitivity and 54.4% specificity in a held-out cohort of 4,996 cases. Dual-stain cytology is the guideline-endorsed triage for HPV-positive screening results but depends on manual reading. The ensemble model was trained on 1,919 cases and evaluated under blinded honest-broker oversight on 9,006 cases in four cohorts, with all preprocessing, aggregation rules and decision parameters fixed before validation. The endpoint was histologically confirmed CIN 3+, or AIN 3+ in an anal cohort, rather than agreement with cytologists, and one classifier served both ThinPrep and SurePath slides without retraining. In the post-lock cohort sensitivity was 88.3% (90% interval 85.3 to 91.3) and specificity 54.4% (52.9 to 55.9); across cohorts the authors report both above ASC-US+ Pap cytology and comparable to or exceeding manual dual-stain reading. Lab: University Medicine Göttingen (with H-Labs and the US National Cancer Institute). Model: Cytoreader-Fusion. Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Eight open problems from Formal Conjectures proved in Lean by a simple agent loop
item.description: A team at FAIR at Meta ran GPT-5.6 Sol in h1, a minimal loop that gives a model a Lean interface and verifier feedback, on 236 problems listed as open in Google DeepMind's Formal Conjectures repository and obtained Lean proofs of eight of them, among them a variant of Erdős Problem 337, three OEIS conjectures and the existence of an AME(9, 10) quantum state; Formal Conjectures marked five as solved. The eight are: W(k)/2ᵏ → ∞ for two-colour van der Waerden numbers, a variant of Erdős 138; the Ruzsa-Turjányi variant of Erdős 337, that |(A + A) ∩ [1, 2N]|/|A ∩ [1, N]| → ∞ for every asymptotic basis of density zero; the OEIS conjectures for A108081, A211417 (Bala's supercongruence, p³ᵏ|a(pᵏ) − a(p^(k − 1)) for primes p ≥ 5) and A022030; the existence of an AME(9, 10) state, a unit vector in (ℂ¹⁰)^(⊗9) whose reduction to any four parties is maximally mixed, which is Open Quantum Problem 35; and Written on the Wall II Conjectures 100 and 314. The proofs were made public on 2026-09-14 in a pull request to Formal Conjectures, merged on 2026-09-24, that marks the first five as solved with links to a repository of nine Lean files; the ninth, Green's Open Problem 25, is not counted in the paper.
